IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
                                  CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
2026 INSC 1113

                            MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION NO.               2026
                                  (@ DIARY NO. 43523 OF 2026)
                                               IN
                                   CIVIL APPEAL NO. 6820 OF 2018

          UNION OF INDIA THROUGH ITS
          SECRETARY & ORS.                                        ... APPLICANTS

                                             VERSUS

          SGT GIRISH KUMAR AND ORS.                           ... RESPONDENTS

                                              ORDER

          1. Delay condoned.

          2. This Miscellaneous Application is filed by the Union of India,

                   seeking clarification of the common judgment dated 12.02.2026

                   passed in C.A. Nos.6820-6824 of 2018 (Union of India Through

                   Its Secretary & Ors. v. SGT Girish Kumar & Ors.) (‘the common

                   judgment’) by which this Court dismissed the appeals preferred

                   by Union of India and allowed the appeals preferred by the ex-

                   servicemen. By the common judgment, ex-servicemen were held

                   entitled to disability pension, including the benefit of broad

                   banding w.e.f. 01.01.1996 or 01.01.2006, as the case may be,

                   along with interest at the rate of 6 % per annum. The objections

                   of the applicant founded on limitation, delay and laches were not
   Signature Not Verified

   Digitally signed by
   BORRA LM VALLI
   Date: 2026.10.12
   16:43:11 IST

                   accepted.
   Reason:




          3. Mrs. Archana Pathak Dave, learned Additional Solicitor General,
                                                                                   1
  submitted that in the batch of appeals decided by this Court vide

  common judgment, the entitlement of Ex-Servicemen to the

  disability element of the pension was never in dispute. It was

  contended that the ex-servicemen in the aforesaid batch of

  appeals were already in receipt of disability pension and had

  merely sought its re-computation by way of broad banding. It was

  urged that the common judgment was rendered in the specific

  factual context of the appeals before this Court and was not

  intended to unsettle the principles governing stale or belated

  pensionary claims.

4. Learned Additional Solicitor General had furnished particulars

  of 23 cases pertaining to Air Force and 26 cases of Army which

  either have been decided or are pending before the High Court or

  the Armed Forces Tribunal (AFT) after the passing of the common

  judgment. It was pointed out that in several cases, the final

  orders passed earlier, which had restricted the benefit of arrears

  and were complied with by the applicant, have been modified by

  placing reliance on the common judgment. It was contended that

  the common judgment is being relied upon in cases involving

  pensionary claims of ex-servicemen which do not fall in the

  category of appeals decided by this Court. It was urged that a

  mechanical application of the common judgment would result in

                                                                   2
  administrative and financial implications and would unsettle the

  matters which have attained finality. It was, therefore, prayed

  that the common judgment be clarified and it be directed that the

  common judgment should not be mechanically extended to all

  pensionary claims where the entitlement of pension itself was in

  dispute and was later settled by Courts/Tribunals.

5. Mr. M.V.R. Mukunda, learned counsel for the respondents, on

  the other hand fairly submitted that in the common judgment,

  arrears from specified dates were granted to ex-servicemen who

  were already in receipt of disability pension and were seeking

  only its re-computation. It was contended that the question of

  delay cannot be examined in isolation from the conduct of Union

  of India. By way of an illustration, it was demonstrated that in a

  case decided by Allahabad High Court, the ex-serviceman retired

  on 31.10.2011 and preferred the appeal claiming disability

  pension on 30.11.2011. It was pointed out that the said appeal

  was decided on 11.02.2017 that is after six years, and thus, the

  original application filed before the Tribunal on 30.04.2018, was

  well within time. It was further pointed out that the applicant

  itself approached court belatedly and therefore cannot claim

  equity on the ground of delay and laches.

6. We have considered the rival submissions and have perused the

                                                                   3
   record.

7. It is well-settled in law that the observations made in a judgment

   are not to be read as provisions of a statute, nor are they to be

   read divorced from the context of the facts in which they were

   made. A difference in facts may make a material difference to the

   precedential value of a decision1.

8. In the light of aforesaid established legal principles, we only wish

   to state that the common judgment dated 12.02.2026 passed in

   Civil Appeal Nos. 6820-6824 of 2018 cannot be construed to

   mean that on the basis of said judgment grant of disability

   pension with arrears can be claimed in every case. Needless to

   state that each claim shall be decided on its own merits.

9. Accordingly, the Miscellaneous Application is disposed of.

                                  ……………..…………………………………J.
                                  [ALOK ARADHE]

NEW DELHI;
October 12, 2026

            4.         Invoking the aforesaid clause, the respondent

                       Analysis

            11.        Before we proceed to interpret the Agreement in

            question for the purposes of determining whether the

            Delhi High Court had the jurisdiction to appoint the

            arbitrator, it would be useful to consider a few decisions

            wherein a distinction between the “seat” of arbitration

            and the “venue” for arbitral proceedings has been carved

            out.

            12.        In Indus Mobile (supra), this Court held that

            seat is akin to an exclusive jurisdiction clause. It was

            held that under the Law of Arbitration, unlike the Code

            of Civil Procedure, which applies to suits filed in courts,

            a reference to “seat” is a concept by which a neutral

            venue can be chosen by the parties to an arbitration

            agreement. The neutral venue may not, in the classical

            sense, have jurisdiction, that is, no part of the cause of

            action may have arisen at the neutral venue, and neither

            would any of the provisions of Sections 16 to 21 of CPC

            be attracted. However, the moment the “seat” is

            determined, the courts wherein the seat is located would


                                                             Page 7 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
                have exclusive jurisdiction for purposes of regulating

                arbitral proceedings arising out of the agreement

                between the parties15.

                13.         In Swastik Gases (supra), the arbitration clause

                in question was clause 17 of the agreement. It was in the

                following terms:

                       “17. Arbitration

                            If any dispute or difference(s) of any kind
                       whatsoever shall arise between the parties hereto in
                       connection with or arising out of this Agreement, the
                       parties hereto shall in good faith negotiate with a view
                       to arriving at an amicable resolution and settlement.
                       In the event no settlement is reached within a period
                       of 30 days from the date of arising of the
                       dispute(s)/difference(s), such dispute(s)/difference(s)
                       shall be referred to 2 (two) Arbitrators, appointed one
                       each by the parties and the Arbitrators, so appointed
                       shall be entitled to appoint a third Arbitrator who
                       shall act as a presiding Arbitrator and the
                       proceedings thereof shall be in accordance with the
                       Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 or any
                       statutory modification or re-enactment thereof in
                       force. The existence of any dispute(s)/difference(s) or
                       initiation/continuation of arbitration proceedings
                       shall not permit the parties to postpone or delay the
                       performance of or to abstain from performing their
                       obligations pursuant to this Agreement.”

                Clause 18 of the agreement conferring jurisdiction

                was in the following terms:

                       “18. Jurisdiction
                       The agreement shall be subject to jurisdiction of the
                       courts at Kolkata.”




15
     Paragraph 19 of the judgment in Indus Mobile (supra)

Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            After considering various decisions, this Court held as

            under:

                  “31. In the instant case, the appellant does not
                  dispute that part of cause of action has arisen in
                  Kolkata. What appellant says is that part of cause of
                  action has also arisen in Jaipur and, therefore, Chief
                  Justice of the Rajasthan High Court or the designate
                  Judge has jurisdiction to consider the application
                  made by the appellant for the appointment of an
                  arbitrator under Section 11. Having regard to Section
                  11(12)(b) and Section 2(e) of the 1996 Act read with
                  Section 20(c) of the Code, there remains no doubt that
                  the Chief Justice or the designate Judge of the
                  Rajasthan High Court has jurisdiction in the matter.
                  The question is, whether parties by virtue of clause
                  18 of the agreement have agreed to exclude the
                  jurisdiction of the courts at Jaipur or, in other words,
                  whether in view of clause 18 of the agreement, the
                  jurisdiction of Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High
                  Court has been excluded?

                  32. For answer to the above question, we have to see
                  the effect of the jurisdiction clause in the agreement
                  which provides that the agreement shall be subject to
                  jurisdiction of the courts at Kolkata. It is a fact that
                  whilst providing for jurisdiction clause in the
                  agreement the words like ‘alone’, ‘only’, ‘exclusive’ or
                  “exclusive jurisdiction” have not been used but this,
                  in our view, is not decisive and does not make any
                  material difference. The intention of the parties - by
                  having Clause 18 in the agreement – is clear and
                  unambiguous that the courts at Kolkata shall have
                  jurisdiction which means that the courts at Kolkata
                  alone shall have jurisdiction. It is so because for
                  construction of jurisdiction clause, like Clause 18 in
                  the agreement, the maxim expressio unius est exclusio
                  alterius comes into play as there is nothing to indicate
                  to the contrary. This legal maxim means that
                  expression of one is the exclusion of another. By
                  making a provision that the agreement is subject to
                  the jurisdiction of the courts at Kolkata, the parties
                  have impliedly excluded the jurisdiction of other
                  courts. Where the contract specifies the jurisdiction
                  of the courts at a particular place and such courts
                  have jurisdiction to deal with the matter, we think
                  that an inference may be drawn that parties intended

                                                                      Page 9 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
                        to exclude all other courts. A clause like this is not hit
                        by Section 23 of the Contract Act at all. Such clause
                        is neither forbidden by law nor it is against the public
                        policy. It does not offend Section 28 of the Contract
                        Act in any manner.”
                                                           (Emphasis supplied)
                14.         In Brahmani River Pellets Ltd. v. Kamachi

                Industries Ltd16, this Court, after considering various

                decisions including Swastik Gases (supra) and Indus

                Mobile (supra), held:

                        “18. Where the contract specifies the jurisdiction of
                        the court at a particular place, only such court will
                        have the jurisdiction to deal with the matter as parties
                        intended to exclude all other courts. In the present
                        case, the parties have agreed that the “venue” of
                        arbitration shall be at Bhubaneswar. Considering the
                        agreement of the parties having Bhubaneswar as the
                        venue of arbitration, the intention of the parties is to
                        exclude all other courts. As held in Swastik, non-use
                        of words like “exclusive jurisdiction”, “only”,
                        “exclusive”, “alone” is not decisive and does not make
                        any material difference.”

                15.         Following      the    decision     of    this    Court     in

                Brahmani           River      Pellets     (supra),     in    Activitas

                Management (supra), this Court set aside the order of

                the High Court of Punjab and Haryana appointing an

                arbitrator in exercise of its power under Section 11 of the

                1996 Act upon finding that clause 10 of the agreement

                relating to the Governing Law had vested exclusive

                jurisdiction to the courts located in Mumbai.


16
     (2020) 5 SCC 462

                                                                             Page 10 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            16.        Clause 10 which was interpreted in Activitas

            Management (supra) provided as under:

                       “10. Governing Law - This letter shall be governed by and
                       construed in accordance with the Indian Law. Client
                       hereby submits to the exclusive jurisdiction of the
                       Mumbai High Courts located in Mumbai in connection
                       with any dispute related to this letter or any of the
                       matters contemplated hereby. In case any dispute arises
                       between the parties with respect to the above-mentioned
                       agreement, parties hereby agree to appoint sole
                       arbitrator by consent of either party as per section 11 of
                       Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and can amicably
                       resolve the dispute as per the procedure laid down in
                       Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 before
                       approaching appropriate court for the same.”

            17.        Interpreting the aforesaid clause, in Activitas

            Management (supra) it was held:

                       “8. Though clause 10 does not use the expression ‘seat’
                       or ‘venue’, we are of the opinion that the ‘jurisdiction’ is
                       mentioned in the context of resolution of the disputes
                       through arbitration and as such the agreement between
                       the parties that, “client hereby submits to the exclusive
                       jurisdiction of the Mumbai High Courts located in Mumbai”
                       must be understood in the context of arbitration and
                       therefore the seat of the arbitration must be taken to be
                       Mumbai.”

            18.        The aforesaid decisions make it clear that

            parties, by agreement, can choose their own place for

            arbitration and may confer exclusive jurisdiction upon

            court(s) located at a particular place for the purpose of

            regulating the arbitral proceedings arising out of the

            agreement between the parties regardless of any part of

            cause of action arising within its territorial jurisdiction.

                                                                       Page 11 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            19.        However, when an agreement specifies the place

            of arbitration and simultaneously confers exclusive

            jurisdiction on courts located at a place other than the

            one specified for arbitration, a question would arise

            whether the place of arbitration is just a “venue” or the

            “juridical seat”.

            20.        In    Arif      Azim   Company       Limited      (supra),

            following an earlier three-Judge Bench judgment of this

            Court in BGS SGS SOMA (supra), a three-Judge Bench

            of this Court delineated the tests as to when “venue” can

            be construed as “seat” of arbitration. The relevant

            paragraphs of the judgment are extracted below:

                       “58. Thus, this court in BGS SJS SOMA laid down a
                       three-condition test as to when “venue” can be construed
                       as “seat” of arbitration. The conditions that are required
                       to be fulfilled are as under:
                              (i)    The arbitration agreement or clause in
                                     question should designate or mention only
                                     one place;
                              (ii)   Such place must have anchored the arbitral
                                     proceedings i.e. the arbitral proceedings
                                     must have been fixed to that place alone
                                     without any scope of change; and
                              (iii) There must be no other significant contrary
                                     indicia to show that the place designated is
                                     merely the venue and not the seat.
                       59. Where the aforesaid conditions are fulfilled, then the
                       place that has been designated as “venue” can be
                       construed as the “seat” of arbitration. It is clarified that,
                       while applying the aforesaid test, it must be borne in
                       mind that where a supranational body of rules has been
                       stipulated in an arbitration agreement or clause, such
                       stipulation is not to be regarded as a contrary indicium,

                                                                       Page 12 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
                       such stipulation does not mean that no seat has been
                       designated rather such stipulation is a positive indicia
                       that the place so designated is actually the “seat”.”



            21.        In the present case, a plain reading of the

            arbitration clause would indicate that Delhi is not the

            only place specified for arbitration. Both Delhi and Goa

            are mentioned as places for holding arbitration. Thus,

            when we apply the tests laid down in BGS SGS SOMA

            (supra), which have been affirmed in Arif Azim (supra),

            the place specified i.e. venue for arbitral proceeding

            would not automatically be the seat of arbitration. In

            such a situation, the Governing Law clause i.e., Clause

            38 of the Agreement would be helpful in determining the

            juridical seat. Since Clause 38 of the Agreement confers

            exclusive jurisdiction to the courts at Goa and Clause

            32.5 provides that arbitration proceedings will be held in

            Goa, it is clear that the parties have agreed that Goa

            shall be the juridical seat, Delhi is just a venue.

            22.        The submission on behalf of the appellant that

            the arbitration agreement is independent of the main

            contract and, therefore, the arbitration clause would

            alone determine the juridical seat, and not the

                                                                   Page 13 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
                Governing Law clause, cannot be countenanced for the

                simple reason that the arbitration clause itself mentions

                two places, namely, Delhi and Goa.            Besides, in

                Mankastu Impex (P) Ltd. v. Airvisual Ltd.17, this Court

                held “that mere expression “place of arbitration” cannot

                be the basis to determine the intention of the parties that

                they have intended that place as the “seat” of arbitration.

                The intention of the parties as to the “seat” should be

                determined from other clauses in the agreement, including

                the conduct of the parties.” Importantly, both Clauses

                32.4 and 32.5 are part of Clause 32 of the Agreement

                which deals with arbitration and dispute resolution.

                According to Clause 32.4, location of the arbitration

                shall be within Delhi; whereas Clause 32.5 states that

                arbitration proceedings will be held in Goa. This creates

                an impression of conflict between the two clauses.

                However, when we construe them harmoniously, to

                ensure that none becomes redundant, and read them in

                conjunction with clause 38 of the Agreement, which




17
     (2020) 5 SCC 399, paragraph 20

                                                                Page 14 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            vests exclusive jurisdiction on courts at Goa, it is clear

            that the juridical seat is at Goa, Delhi is just a venue.

            23.        Now we shall consider the decisions cited by the

            learned counsel for the respondent. In Sasan Power

            (supra), this Court held that arbitration agreement is an

            independent agreement, and the arbitration clause is

            not the one that governs rights and obligations arising

            out of the substantive contract rather it only governs the

            way of settling disputes between the parties. It was also

            held that parties can agree upon the governing law but

            may not have any agreement for settlement of dispute

            through arbitration. There can be no quarrel with the

            aforesaid proposition. Here, the arbitration clause itself

            mentions two places. One of those two has been chosen

            by the parties for the courts located therein to have

            exclusive jurisdiction. In such a situation, to determine

            the juridical seat, the Governing law clause 38 cannot

            be ignored.         Similarly, in the Delhi High Court decision

            in M/s. Cable Corporation of India (supra), the

            arbitration clause specifies only a single place and not

            two places as is there in the present case. The said


                                                                 Page 15 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            decision is therefore distinguishable. In the other

            decision of the Delhi High Court rendered in Sunil

            Kumar Chandra (supra), which has been cited on

            behalf of the respondent, the arbitration clause has not

            been extracted in the judgment. However, from the

            judgment, it appears that one of the clauses of the

            agreement made it clear that Delhi was chosen as the

            seat of arbitration, but it was not clear whether the other

            place specified therein was for arbitration. This decision

            too is, therefore, distinguishable. Besides, here the

            arbitration        clause      itself   specifies   two   places    for

            arbitration. The Constitution Bench decision of this

            Court in Ramkishorelal (supra) is on the general

            principle that to construe an instrument, an effort must

            be there to ascertain the intention of the parties after

            considering all words. We fail to understand as to how

            this decision would be of any help to the respondent. In

            Shree Bhowani Cotton Mills (supra), another decision

            cited on behalf of the respondent, it was held that mere

            conferment of exclusive jurisdiction on courts at

            Calcutta to entertain and try suits in respect of any


                                                                       Page 16 of18
Civil Appeal @ SLP (C) No. 35915 of 2025
            claims or disputes would not nullify the arbitration

            agreement. In the present case, there is no issue about

            the existence of an arbitration agreement and, further,

            there is no dispute that the arbitration agreement itself

            specifies two places, namely, Delhi and Goa; in such

            circumstances, in our view, the juridical seat would have

            to be ascertained by reading the Agreement in its

            entirety so as to decipher the true intention of the

            parties.       The last judgment relied on behalf of the

            respondent is one rendered by the Karnataka High Court

            in M/s Lyrus Life Sciences (supra). The said decision

            holds that where precise location of arbitration is

            specified as Bengaluru, the argument that the cause of

            action had arisen in the State of Himachal Pradesh

            would not be relevant for the purposes of arbitration.

            This decision is of no relevance to the present case

            because the arbitration clause itself specifies both Delhi

            and Goa for arbitration. Therefore, whether the juridical

            seat is Delhi or Goa would have to be ascertained on the

            basis of intention of the parties as could be evinced from

            a holistic reading of various clauses of the Agreement.

4.          The issue is with respect to whether the 2nd and 3rd

respondents must be included in the arbitration; whom, if we

find to be veritable parties on a prima facie consideration of

the facts and circumstances, still the question would be open

before the Arbitrator appointed.

5.          The High Court, considering the application under

Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 19961, first

considered the aspect of limitation, especially since there

was an earlier Arbitral Award at the instance of the appellants

themselves, which was set aside under Section 34 of the said

Act. The question of limitation was found in favour of the

appellants, which we need not engage with, especially since

the issue of limitation is deemed to have been answered only

as against 1st and 2nd respondents; and with respect to 3rd and

4th respondents, prayer to join them in the arbitration was

declined. The rejection of such prayer was also on account of

the finding that they are not signatories to the Arbitration

as person/persons claiming through or under a signatory or

covered under the Group of Companies doctrine.

6.      We would first look at the facts which led to the

application before the High Court. The dispute specifically

arises with respect to a property numbered as Unit No.2

admeasuring 3,500 sq. ft. in the ground floor of Manish

Commercial Centre, 216-A, Dr. Annie Besant Road, Worli,

Mumbai - 400 030, which is hereinafter termed as the ‘subject

asset’. This originally belonged to a partnership firm called

M/s Prospective Traders. The original deed of partnership

was executed between three family trusts, respectively of V.

U. Shah, N.U. Shah and C.U. Shah; who are referred to as the

original partners, by a deed of partnership executed on

02.04.1977. The asset was acquired by the partnership on

03.10.1977. On 09.12.1985, the partnership was reconstituted

by a deed, wherein the appellants; Hemant D. Shah HUF and

the wife of Hemant D. Shah, the 1st and 2nd appellants as also

Chittaranjan D. Shah HUF and the daughter in law of C.D.

Shah, the 1st and 2nd respondents were inducted as partners.

7.      Subsequently on 30.12.1987, by another deed of

partnership; which is also disputed by the appellants, the

partnership firm was reconstituted and the original partners

retired. On 03.07.1995, by a deed of retirement, the

appellants are asserted to have retired from the partnership
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                       Page 3 of 10
firm, which document is alleged to be a forged one by the

appellants. Later, on 01.07.2005, the 2nd respondent retired

from the partnership firm, resulting in dissolution of the said

partnership firm and it continued as a proprietorship with its

assets vested with the 1st respondent. Again, by a deed of

30.09.2009, 3rd and 4th respondents were brought as partners

into the proprietorship, constituting a new partnership. On

retirement of the 1st respondent, by a deed of 04.11.2009, 3rd

and 4th respondents continued as partners of the firm.

8.          The 3rd and 4th respondents distanced themselves

from the partnership agreement of 09.12.1985; which

contains an arbitration clause and the 1st and 2nd respondents

assert the dissolution of the firm on the retirement of 2nd

respondent, subsequent to the retirement of the appellants.

The appellants, on the other hand, assert that they never

retired from the firm and the partnership continues even

now, as also the assets belong to the original partnership.

9.          Learned Single Judge has relied on Cox & Kings

Limited v. SAP India Private Limited and Another2 and




 2
     (2024) 4 SCC 1
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                       Page 4 of 10
Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited v. BCL Secure

Premises Private Limited3.

10.         Cox & Kings Limited2 elaborately considered the

principle of ‘claiming through or under’ and the ‘doctrine of

group companies’, which we are of the opinion, does not

apply to the present proceedings. However, the principle

stated therein would assist us in resolving the question raised

herein, which has to be resolved on the facts arising in the

present case. Holding arbitration law to be an autonomous

legal field, there was a distinction drawn from the corporate

law and contract law, insofar as the main purpose of the latter

is imputation of substantive legal liability while the law of

arbitration determines whether an Arbitration Tribunal has

jurisdiction over the disputes arising between the parties to

an arbitration agreement. A non-signatory, who has not put

pen to paper, indicates an intention, not to assume rights or

responsibilities under the agreement. But, it was held that

the Courts and Tribunals cannot adopt a rigid approach to

exclude all persons or entities, who through conduct and

relationship with the signatories intended to be bound by the



 3
     (2026) 3 SCC 711
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                       Page 5 of 10
underlying contract containing the arbitration clause (para

100).

11.     It was held in paragraph 132 of Cox & Kings Limited 2

that ‘Looking at the factors holistically, it could be inferred that

the non-signatories, by virtue of their relationship with the

signatory parties and active involvement in the performance of

commercial obligations which are intricately linked to the

subject-matter, are not actually strangers to the dispute

between the signatory parties.’(sic)

12.     From the conclusion of Cox & Kings Ltd.2, we extract

paragraphs 170.3, 170.12 and 170.13 as under:

        ‘170.3. The requirement of a written arbitration
        agreement under Section 7 does not exclude the
        possibility of binding non-signatory parties;
        xxx                   xxx                     xxx
        170.12. At the referral stage, the referral court
        should leave it for the Arbitral Tribunal to decide
        whether the non-signatory is bound by the
        arbitration agreement; and
        170.13. In the course of this judgment, any
        authoritative determination given by this Court
        pertaining to the Group of Companies doctrine
        should not be interpreted to exclude the
        application of other doctrines and principles for
        binding non-signatories to the arbitration
        agreement.’

13.     Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited3 referred

to Cox & Kings Limited2 and culled out the principle of a

prima facie satisfaction being entered by the Referral Court,
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                            Page 6 of 10
that there exists an Arbitration Agreement and the non-

signatory being a veritable party. It was found that despite

such prima facie satisfaction entered, the jurisdiction of the

Arbitral Tribunal to decide on it, on the basis of factual

evidence and the application of legal doctrine, is preserved.

However, it was held that the Referral Court under Section 11

of the Act is not deprived of its jurisdiction from examining

whether the non-signatory, in the real sense, is a party to the

agreement, the answer to which will depend on the facts and

circumstances        of   each   case.   Therein   the   appellant

Corporation floated a tender, the successful tenderer in

which gave a sub-contract to the respondent. There was a

civil suit and later an arbitration attempted by the sub-

contractor to settle the disputes with the original contractor.

That having failed, the sub-contractor filed an application

under Section 11 of the Act against the appellant Corporation,

which stood allowed. In the factual scenario, it was found that

there was not even a semblance of an intent to affect a legal

relationship between the sub-contractor and the awarder or

that such a third party was a veritable party.

14.     Be that as it may, in the present case, the dispute

revolves around the ‘subject asset’ which is an immovable
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                            Page 7 of 10
property. Admittedly, the asset was acquired by the

partnership firm, in which, later the appellants and the 1st and

2nd respondents were partners, along with the original

partners. The original partners retired and though the said

document is disputed by the appellants, the original partners

do not raise any dispute on the said document. The

retirement of the original partners also does not affect the

rights of the appellants, if the deed of 09.12.1985 subsists.

The bone of contention is the deed of retirement dated

03.07.1995, by which the appellants are said to have retired;

which is alleged to be a forged document.

15.     In fact, it is this retirement which led to the eventual

constitution of another partnership by the 1st and 2nd

respondents; subsequently with the retirement of 2nd

respondent, the firm continued as a proprietorship with the

1st respondent, who inducted 3rd and 4th respondents and

then retired from the firm. If the deed of retirement of

03.07.1995 is found to be invalid on the allegations raised,

then necessarily the parties revert to the partnership of

09.12.1985. In which event, it would affect the rights of the 3rd

and 4th respondents, who were inducted by the 1st

respondent, as partners who obtained rights over the
 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                         Page 8 of 10
‘subject asset’ by that partnership deed, in which neither the

appellants nor the 1st and 2nd respondents are partners. The

dispute raised for arbitration revolves around the ownership

of the ‘subject asset’; whether it be by virtue of the deed of

09.12.1985 or by the deed of 04.11.2009.

16.     On the facts and circumstances of this case, we are of

the opinion that 3rd and 4th respondents are veritable parties

to the dispute, since it would substantially affect their rights

also as per the partnership deed of 30.11.2009 which can be

valid only if the deed of retirement of the appellants is valid.

However, this is not to say that the questions of limitation

raised by 3rd and 4th respondents and whether the appellants

are estopped from including 3rd and 4th respondents, as they

were not included in the earlier arbitration proceedings,

despite knowledge of the retirement deed at that point of

time, would not survive. These aspects are definitely left to

be agitated before the Arbitral Tribunal.

17.     The impugned order is modified only to the extent of

finding the 3rd and 4th respondents to be veritable parties to

the arbitration, despite the said respondents being not

signatories to the partnership deed of 09.12.1985.


 CA@ SLP (C) No.26474 of 2026                        Page 9 of 10
18.     We hasten to observe that our findings on 3rd and 4th

respondents being veritable parties, is a prima facie finding,

which would not govern the adjudication of the said issue or

the issue of limitation or the ground raised of an estoppel

against the appellants by 3rd and 4th respondents, which

would be alive; left to be considered by the Arbitral Tribunal.

19.     With the above observations and modification to the

impugned order, the appeal stands disposed of.

20.     Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

4.       Learned Counsel for the appellant points out that the

rejection was only on the ground that the appellant had not

submitted the original of the Bid Security furnished, which in

the case of the appellant was submitted through the e-

payment Gateway of Authority. The Bid Security was remitted

5.       Learned A.S.G. for the respondent-Ministry of

Railways, however, points out that Clause 2.20.6(ii)

specifically requires the original to be submitted, and in that

circumstance, the rejection was proper. Learned Counsel for

the 3rd respondent relied on the decision in Prakash

Asphaltings and Toll Highways (India) Ltd. v. Mandeepa

Enterprises and Others1 to argue that the awarder is the best

equipped to understand and appreciate its requirements and

interpret bid documents and the Constitutional Courts should

defer to such understanding and appreciation of the tender

documents. There is no elbow room insofar as producing the

original documents, is the 3rd respondent’s contention.

6.       Learned Counsel for the appellant also points out that

his financial bid was far lower than that of the 3rd respondent

and this causes loss to the exchequer. Learned A.S.G. alertly

points out that there was no opportunity to compare the

financial bids, since the appellant had failed in its technical

bid at the inception, for non-production of the required

original receipt, and in that circumstance, the appellant’s

financial bid was never opened.

7.       Clause 2.20.6 of the RFP, produced as Annexure P1,

speaks of submission of Bid Security in the form of Bank

Guarantee/ Account Payee Demand Draft/Fixed Deposit

Receipt/ Banker's Cheque/ e-payment Gateway of Authority.

It is also stipulated in Clause 1 that a scanned copy of the

same shall be uploaded on e-Procurement Portal while

applying for the tender. There is no dispute that the appellant

made payment of the Bid Security by means of e-payment

and the rejection was only on the ground of violation of

Clause (ii). Clause (ii) prescribes that the form in which the

Bid Security is furnished, should be delivered in person,

physically, to the official nominated, as indicated in the

tender document. The appellant’s contention is that there is

no question of production of an original, since the payment

has already gone into the coffers of the respondents and the

digital receipt has been uploaded along with the tender

document.

8.       We are perfectly in agreement with the contention of

the appellant, especially looking at the various forms in

which the Bid Security can be furnished; a Bank Guarantee/

Account Payee Demand Draft/Fixed Deposit Receipt/

Banker's Cheque, unless physically furnished to the

respondent, there can be no lien exercised on the Bid

Security. It is, hence, the stipulation that at the time of

application, the scanned copy should be uploaded and later

the original should be handed over to the nominated official.

 CA@ SLP (C) No.25855 of 2026                         Page 4 of 7
Insofar as the appellant is concerned, the money was

deposited to the account of the respondents and there is

nothing further required to be produced insofar as the e-

payment made, especially when the digital payment receipt

had been uploaded along with the bid document.

9.       Prakash Asphaltings and Toll Highways (India) Ltd.1

was a case in which a tender was invited for toll collection.

When the financial bid was opened, tenderers whose

technical bid was found to be qualified; three of them, had

quoted in crores while one had quoted a paltry amount of

Rs.9,72,999/-. The contention raised was that this was a bona

fide mistake, and the financial bid indicated only the

collection of a single day and if it is worked out for the total

contract of 1095 days, it would be Rs.100.65 crores and then

their bid would be the highest. It was in this context that this

Court held that the words used in the tender documents

cannot be ignored or treated as redundant or superfluous.

The tenderer was required to give the total collection for the

contract period and an omission insofar as submitting a paltry

amount, even if inadvertent, cannot be explained by putting

forth the contention that the bid was mistakenly quoted at the

 CA@ SLP (C) No.25855 of 2026                          Page 5 of 7
per day rate. It is also pertinent that this Court in the aforesaid

decision, while cautioning the Constitutional Court’s to defer

to the understanding and appreciation of the tender

documents, also carved out an exception insofar as mala fide

and perverse understanding or appreciation                 of the

documents, especially in the application of the terms of the

tender document.

10.      We are convinced that here, there is a clear

perversity; insofar as an e-payment was made, as required

by the tender document, the digital receipt of which was

scanned and uploaded, rejected only since the original was

not produced; which is an impossibility. Rigid adherence to

the letter of a document cannot be countenanced, especially

when there is a clear impossibility in compliance of the same.

As we noticed, Bid Security, when furnished in all other

forms, cannot be enforced, unless the original comes into the

hands of the respondents. However, insofar as the e-payment

is concerned, the money has already been transferred to the

account of the respondents, and they have full control over it.

11.      We, hence, set aside the impugned order and direct

the contract to be awarded to the appellant herein.
